title: ASTs & Semantic Analysis
summary: What happens after parsing but before code generation: collapsing a noisy parse tree into a usable AST, then checking that a structurally valid program actually makes sense.

slides.markdown:
[parsing-and-grammars](parsing-and-grammars) proves a token stream is *structurally* valid — it matches the grammar. That's a much weaker claim than "this program makes sense." `"a" + 3` in a statically typed language parses perfectly: it's a well-formed addition expression. It's still nonsense, and semantic analysis is the stage that catches exactly that gap.

Two things happen here, and they're related but distinct: the noisy **parse tree** the parser produced gets collapsed into a cleaner **AST** that drops grammar scaffolding nobody downstream needs, and then that AST gets walked to check **scope** (does this name refer to anything?) and **types** (does this operation make sense on these types?).

This is the stage most interview "why doesn't this compile" questions are actually about — undeclared variables, type mismatches, and shadowing bugs all live here, not in parsing.

slides.subTitle: Why compilers discard grammar noise
slides.markdown:
A parse tree is a faithful record of every grammar rule the parser applied — including non-terminals that exist purely to make the grammar's precedence and associativity work, and punctuation tokens (`(`, `;`, `,`) that mattered for parsing but carry no meaning once structure is established.

An **AST** (Abstract Syntax Tree) keeps only what later stages actually need: the operation, and its operands. Parentheses in `(2 + 3) * 4` are essential to the parse tree's shape — they're literally why multiplication doesn't just eat the `3` — but once the AST correctly nests `Add(2, 3)` inside `Mul(_, 4)`, the parenthesis tokens themselves have done their job and are dropped. "Abstract" means exactly this: structure that matters, stripped of the concrete syntax that produced it.

slides.sectionTitle: A parse tree collapsing into an AST
slides.markdown:
![Parse tree collapsing into a minimal AST for 2 + 3 * 4](assets/parse-tree-vs-ast.svg)

The AST is smaller and flatter than the parse tree it was built from, and that's the point — everything the grammar needed to disambiguate precedence has already done its work and can be discarded, leaving just the semantic content: what operation, on what operands, in what order.

slides.subTitle: Tracking declarations and resolving names
slides.markdown:
A **symbol table** maps each declared name to the information the compiler needs about it: its type, the scope it belongs to, its memory location or register once that's decided later in the pipeline. Every declaration (`int x`, `function foo(...)`) adds an entry; every use of a name (`x + 1`) triggers a lookup against the table to find what that name actually refers to.

This is the concrete mechanism behind "is this variable declared": if a lookup finds no entry for a name in any enclosing scope, that's an **undeclared variable** error — the single most common semantic error message, and the most mechanical to explain, because it's a literal table-miss.

Symbol tables are usually implemented as a **chain of scopes** — one table per nested block, each pointing to its enclosing scope's table. A name lookup checks the innermost scope first, then walks outward, stopping at the first match.

That "stop at the first match" rule is exactly what **shadowing** is: an inner-scope declaration with the same name as an outer one doesn't error, it just wins the lookup for any code inside that inner scope, and the outer variable becomes unreachable there without being destroyed. This is deliberate and common (`for (int i = 0; ...) { int i = compute(); }` is legal, if confusing, in most languages) — but it's also a well-known source of real bugs, where a developer means to reference the outer variable and silently gets the shadowed inner one instead, with no error anywhere, because both lookups are individually valid.

slides.sectionTitle: Type checking as a tree walk
slides.markdown:
Type checking walks the AST bottom-up (or via a recursive function mirroring the tree's structure) computing a type for every subexpression and validating that each operator's operand types are actually compatible with what that operator requires. `Add(a, b)`'s type checker asks: what's the type of `a`, what's the type of `b`, and does this specific language's `+` accept that combination — and if not, that's a **type error**, reported at exactly the AST node where the mismatch occurs.

This is genuinely just tree traversal plus a lookup table of "which operators accept which type combinations" — the same shape of algorithm as computing any other bottom-up property of a tree, applied to a specific, language-defined rule set.

The pitfall this topic is built to name: conflating **syntactic** validity (matches the grammar) with **semantic** validity (means something coherent). A program can be perfectly, unambiguously parseable and still be entirely wrong — wrong types, undeclared names, calling a function with the wrong number of arguments, using a value before it's assigned.

This distinction is exactly why compiler error output is organized into phases: a syntax error and a type error are different categories of mistake with different fixes, and a compiler that reported both under one generic "error" bucket would be strictly less useful. Recognizing which category an error belongs to — before trying to fix it — is the practical skill this whole topic distills into.

slides.sectionTitle: Caught at compile time here, not there
slides.markdown:
"Why is this variable 'undefined' caught at compile time here, but not there" is really asking about the difference between statically and dynamically typed (or scoped) languages' semantic analysis passes.

A statically typed, statically scoped language (Java, Rust, Go) runs a full symbol-table pass over the whole program *before* it ever executes, so an undeclared variable is a guaranteed compile error — the check happens once, exhaustively, across every code path, including ones that would never actually run at runtime given the actual input. A dynamically typed language (Python, JavaScript) often defers name resolution to execution — a name lookup failing only fails when that specific line actually runs, so an undefined variable inside a branch that's never taken in a given run can silently exist in the source, undetected, until that exact input finally exercises it. Same underlying bug category, different point in time the check happens — and that timing difference is the entire answer to this question.

A program that survives semantic analysis is now known to be both structurally valid *and* meaningful under the language's rules — every name resolves, every operation's types check out. The AST itself is usually **annotated** at this point: each node gets tagged with its resolved type and, often, a direct reference to the symbol-table entry it resolved to, so later stages never have to redo this work.

That annotated tree is exactly what [intermediate-representations](intermediate-representations) starts from — lowering a tree that already knows its own types and bindings into a flatter, more uniform IR that the back end can optimize and eventually turn into real instructions.

slides.sectionTitle: The line between structure and meaning
slides.markdown:
The clean way to hold this topic in your head: parsing answers "is this shaped right," semantic analysis answers "does this make sense." Both questions have to get a yes before a program is allowed anywhere near code generation, and they're checked by genuinely different mechanisms — grammar rules for the first, symbol tables and type rules for the second.

Every "why won't this compile" question that isn't about a missing bracket or semicolon is a semantic-analysis question, and reaching for the right mental model — scope lookup failure versus type incompatibility versus something else — is most of what answering it well looks like.
